The topic 'Standard output and formatted printing' introduces standard_output.

[0] everyday_reading (E): In maths `7.2` (or %2.4f) reads as a decimal number, or as '7 digits before the point, 2 after'. In a format specifier the number before the point is the total field width and the number after it is the digits after the decimal point. Also `%` is not 'percent'.
[1] misconception (M) -> PrintfAnyConversion: wrong rule: Any conversion code (%d, %f, %s) works with any argument type. Right rule: The conversion must fit the argument's type (%s accepts any type). printf("%12d", Math.PI) or printf("%4.2f", 512) throws IllegalFormatConversionException at run time.
[2] misconception (M) -> FieldWidthIsIntegerDigits: wrong rule: %2.4f prints two digits before the decimal point and four after. Right rule: The first number is the width of the whole field. %7.2f means 7 characters in total, with 2 digits after the decimal point.
[3] misconception (M) -> PrintfAddsNewline: wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string.
[4] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PrintfAnyConversion: Points to LT (specifiers are paired with arguments left to right, and the other characters pass through). An uneven trace pairs a specifier with the wrong argument, drops the literal text between specifiers, or pads on the wrong side on some fields. (here mixing in: "Any conversion code (%d, %f, %s) works with any argument type")
[5] misconception (M) -> ManyDigitsMeanAccurate: wrong rule: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. Right rule: Printing precision is only formatting. A value printed to many places can still be inaccurate, and ensuring accuracy is the hard part.

[0] names_the_element (N): printf is the formatted-print method of standard output. It takes a format string and arguments and writes the formatted string.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A format specifier has the form %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion: d for integer types, f for floating-point values, s for String or any type. The width is a minimum character count, and for f the precision is the number of digits after the point.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): The arguments are evaluated first. The format string is then scanned left to right: ordinary characters are copied, and each specifier takes the next argument, converts it, rounds it to the precision and pads it with blanks to the width (left side by default, right side with the `-` flag).
[1] output_prediction (OP): The output is the formatted text. printf("%7.5f", Math.PI) gives 3.14159, printf("PI is approximately %.2f\n", Math.PI) gives `PI is approximately 3.14` and a newline, and printf("%5d", 42) gives `   42`. Rounding is half-up.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One call appends one formatted string to standard output and adds no newline unless \n or %n is in the format. The stored values of the arguments do not change (only their printed form is rounded).

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): printf output goes into the same stream as print/println and lands at the point in the stream where it was called. It does not end the line.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): println prints a double with all its digits (about 15 places) and always ends the line. printf("%.2f\n", x) controls the digits and ends the line only because of \n.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: table printing. Inside a loop, one fixed format string with a specifier per column prints aligned rows (e.g. a loan table) at a chosen precision.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PrintfAnyConversion: Changing the precision changes only the printed digits, not the stored value. Changing the width changes only the padding. A width smaller than the converted text is ignored, so nothing is truncated.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use printf when the number of digits, the field width or column alignment matters (tables, money, reports). For quick checks of a value, println is enough.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The conversion code must match the argument type. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: %d with a double, or %f with an int (e.g. printf("%4.2f", 512)): IllegalFormatConversionException.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: There must be an argument for every specifier, and the format syntax must be legal. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: More specifiers than arguments (e.g. printf("%d %d", 3)), or a malformed specifier: an IllegalFormatException subclass such as MissingFormatArgumentException.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: printf adds no line separator. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A printf in a loop without \n: all rows run together on one line.

println prints each number with all its digits and ends the line; printf formats each value by its conversion code and starts a new line only when \n is in the format string.
printf writes to standard output, like print, but formats each value first.
